name: NE555 Timer
summary: The timer that refuses to die. Monostable, astable or Schmitt comparator depending on how you wire the three resistor-divider taps. Pin 1 is just left of the notch.
notes: The internal divider sets the thresholds at 1/3 VCC (trigger) and 2/3 VCC (threshold). Everything the chip does follows from those two numbers.
Astable frequency is f ≈ 1.44 / ((R1 + 2·R2)·C), duty cycle = (R1 + R2) / (R1 + 2·R2). A duty cycle below 50% needs a diode across R2.
Monostable pulse width is t ≈ 1.1 · R · C.
RESET (pin 4) is active low and must be tied to VCC if unused, or the timer will not run.
Decouple CONTROL (pin 5) to ground with 10 nF unless you are modulating it. Leaving it bare is the most common cause of a jittery 555.
The bipolar NE555 pulls a current spike of 100-200 mA through its supply on every output transition. Put 100 nF across VCC and GND at the chip, and prefer the CMOS TLC555 near anything analog.

The output is a totem pole that swings to within about 1.7 V of VCC on a bipolar 555, and does not reach ground either. Driving a MOSFET gate from a 5 V 555 is marginal; use the CMOS TLC555 or a gate driver.

pins.name: TRIG
pins.note: Output goes high while this sits below 1/3 VCC. Edge-triggered in monostable mode.

pins.name: OUT
pins.note: Sources or sinks up to 200 mA, enough to drive a small relay or speaker directly.

pins.name: RESET
pins.note: Tie to VCC when unused. Pulling it low forces the output low regardless of the timing network.

pins.name: CTRL
pins.note: Sits at 2/3 VCC. Drive it to make a voltage-controlled oscillator, or decouple with 10 nF.

pins.name: THRES
pins.note: Output goes low once this rises above 2/3 VCC.

pins.name: DISCH
pins.note: Dumps the timing capacitor. In astable mode R2 connects here.

pins.name: VCC
pins.note: 16 V is the recommended max on the NE555 and 18 V the absolute max. The TLC555 runs from 2 V.

circuit.title: Astable oscillator

parts.why: Charges the timing capacitor through R1 and R2.
Discharges through R2 alone, which is why duty cycle is always over 50 percent.
Ties the two comparators to the same node. This is what makes it free-run.
Sets the period together with R1 and R2.
Stops the internal divider picking up noise. The usual cause of a jittery 555.
Held low the timer simply will not run.
The bipolar 555 pulls a 100 to 200 mA spike through the supply on every output transition.

circuit.note: Frequency is about 1.44 / ((R1 + 2 x R2) x C). For a duty cycle under 50 percent put a diode across R2.
